newsitem.title: USA: WHX says strike could mean steel co's end.
newsitem.headline: WHX says strike could mean steel co's end.

text.p: The strike against WHX Corp by the United Steelworkers union could put its steel operations out of business in one year if the labor dispute is not resolved, WHX Chairman Ron LaBow said Tuesday.
"I think no one has ever told the union to 'stuff it' before," LaBow told Reuters. "The steel industry is notorious for that but we're fighting back."
"I think they run the risk of putting the company out of business in a year," he said. "I think the strike will go on for another six to 12 months at a minimum."
Union officials were not available for comment.
Some 4,700 workers have been on strike at WHX's Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel unit since October 1, idling eight plants in Pennsylvania, West Virginia and Ohio.
WHX's interests are primarily in steel but the New York-based holding company also owns a casino and dog track and a building products company.

The dispute centers around pensions. The union wants WHX to use its $400 million in cash-on-hand to establish a defined benefit plan, under which funding is guaranteed and based on wages and length of service.

"We're not giving them a defined benefit plan," LaBow said. "It busted the company once and it will bust it again." The company at one time had an underfunded defined benefit plan, which helped push it into bankruptcy in 1985.

The company emerged from bankruptcy in 1991 and now operates a defined contribution plan, under which a percentage of a worker's pay is put into an investment fund and benefits paid depend on the fund's performance.

LaBow said the company's offer to enhance that plan actually exceeds what the union wants in terms of payments. "If a guy is 45, works another 15 years and retires at 60...if (his pay percentage) is invested in government bonds, he'll get about $2,500 to $3,000 a month. That's double what the union is asking."
LaBow also said WHX needs its cash-on-hand for capital expenditures, debt payments and possible acquisitions.

"We've offered a wage package that's above the rest of the industry, signing bonuses...I think the union leaders should let the rank-and-file vote on our offer. If they voted today, our offer would be approved overwhelmingly."
Negotiators for the two sides met last Friday in Pittsburgh under the supervision of a federal mediator.
In a news release issued late Friday, the union said the company rejected its proposal to combine elements of both a defined benefit and a defined contribution plan.
The union's strike fund has been paying each worker an average of $115 a week, according to union officials. The union also operates a food bank and has been distributing food staples to workers.
No further talks are scheduled. While declining to elaborate, LaBow said the company is considering "a number of options" to cushion itself against the costly impact of a prolonged strike.

Industry sources have speculated recently that WHX could eventually shut down or sell its steel melting operations, commonly called the "hot end," and continue operating only its rolling and finishing operations, commonly called "downstream."
